analysis.one_liner: Raises minimum fines for oil and hazardous spills into U.S. waters, up to $250 per barrel.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after one Senate hearing in July 1989, the Environment and Public Works Committee never voted on it, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Clean Water Act's spill penalties so that the EPA could fine companies that discharge oil or hazardous substances into U.S. waters at least $50,000, and up to $50 for every barrel spilled — rising to at least $250,000 and up to $250 per barrel when a company's own willful misconduct caused the spill. Current law at the time capped these penalties; this bill would replace the ceiling with a floor. It would also require the EPA to report to Congress every two years on whether the nation's oil spill response plans are adequate.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near, use, or depend on U.S. waters — coastal communities, fishermen, and water users — who get stronger deterrence against oil and chemical spills and annual-to-biennial public reporting on how well spill response plans actually work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities, fishermen, and water users

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the current penalty ceiling with a minimum fine of $50,000 and up to $50 per barrel discharged, so small fines stop being an affordable cost of doing business [S2][S3].

Raises the penalty to at least $250,000 and up to $250 per barrel when a spill resulted from willful negligence or willful misconduct by the owner or operator, with each violation counted as a separate offense [S3].

Requires the EPA, consulting with the Coast Guard's department, to report to Congress every two years assessing whether the National Contingency Plan and spill-response regulations are adequate, and to recommend improvements [S2][S3].

Allows penalties to be pursued in federal district court where the defendant is located or does business, and requires the EPA to weigh the violator's ability to stay in business and its mitigation efforts when setting the amount [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil transporters, tanker operators, and other companies that discharge oil or hazardous substances into U.S. waters would face substantially higher fines, and those costs can flow into shipping and fuel prices; EPA and the courts would take on new enforcement and reporting work.

drawbacks.text: The flat $50,000 minimum applies regardless of how small the discharge is, which could be disproportionate for a small operator's minor violation even though the bill lets the EPA consider the size of the business [S3].
Higher expected liability raises operating costs for oil transport and spill-prone industries, and some of that cost would likely be passed on to consumers in fuel and shipping prices [S3].
The bill leaves in place other limits on liability for spill damages elsewhere in the law, so it stiffens fines without creating a comprehensive spill-liability regime [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but moderate: tougher fines and mandatory reviews of spill-response adequacy would strengthen deterrence in a period when oil spills were a live national concern. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and partly on consumers through prices, and the one-size minimum fine is blunt for minor violations. On balance the bill modestly favored the public, but it was a narrow enforcement measure, not a comprehensive overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 1989, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in July 1989, and then sat there until the Congress ended in January 1991 without ever being voted on.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus, joined by Sens. George Mitchell and Frank Lautenberg, introduced the bill on April 4, 1989 [S1][S3].
Four senators — two Democrats and two Republicans — cosponsored it [S4].
The Senate referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
The Subcommittee on Environmental Protection held hearings on July 21, 1989, printed as S.Hrg. 101-272 [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that transport and discharge oil and hazardous substances are better off, because they continued to face the old penalty ceilings rather than a $50,000 minimum and per-barrel fines of up to $250 a barrel.

sides.party_line_note: The three original sponsors were Democrats, but the four cosponsors split evenly between the parties (two Democrats, two Republicans), and no recorded vote ever tested opposition.

industries.industry: Oil transport and shipping (tanker operators, oil handlers)
industries.note: The bill would have raised spill penalties from a capped amount to a $50,000 minimum and up to $50 per barrel — $250 per barrel for willful misconduct — making spills significantly more expensive for the companies that cause them. Its death meant those companies kept the old, lower penalty ceilings.
The bill extends the per-barrel penalty structure to hazardous-substance discharges as well, exposing chemical dischargers to the same higher fines. It never passed, so no change took effect.
